input:
Write a bash script that splits file paths into parts.

Starting files:
--- /home/eval/data/paths.txt ---
/var/log/nginx/access.log
/home/eval/archive.tar.gz
/etc/hosts
relative/dir/README
/home/eval/.bashrc
/opt/app/v1.2/run.sh
--- end ---

For each path, in order, write one line `DIR|BASE|STEM|EXT` to /home/eval/data/parts.txt:
- DIR: everything before the last `/` (every path here contains a `/`);
- BASE: everything after the last `/`;
- EXT: the text after the last `.` in BASE, or empty when BASE has no `.` other than a leading one (e.g. `.bashrc` has no extension);
- STEM: BASE without `.EXT` (BASE itself when EXT is empty).
Exit 0.

transcript.final_response:
Edge cases to handle:

- `/etc/hosts` has DIR `/etc`.
- A path like `/foo` would give an empty DIR, but none of the inputs here is like that.
- `.bashrc` has a leading dot only, so EXT is empty and STEM is `.bashrc`.
- `archive.tar.gz` gives EXT `gz` and STEM `archive.tar`.
- `v1.2` is in the DIR, not the BASE, so it doesn't affect EXT.

The script uses parameter expansion. DIR is `${p%/*}` and BASE is `${p##*/}`. To decide whether BASE has an extension, strip the leading dot with `rest="${base#.}"`. If `rest` contains a `.`, then EXT is `${base##*.}` and STEM is `${base%.*}`. Otherwise EXT is empty and STEM is BASE.

A name like `..foo` is not in the input, so I don't handle it specially. The loop also skips an empty last line, using `|| [[ -n $p ]]` to cover a missing trailing newline.

```bash
#!/bin/bash
in=/home/eval/data/paths.txt
out=/home/eval/data/parts.txt
: > "$out"
while IFS= read -r p || [[ -n $p ]]; do
  [[ -z $p ]] && continue
  dir="${p%/*}"
  base="${p##*/}"
  rest="${base#.}"
  if [[ $rest == *.* ]]; then
    ext="${base##*.}"
    stem="${base%.*}"
  else
    ext=""
    stem="$base"
  fi
  printf '%s|%s|%s|%s\n' "$dir" "$base" "$stem" "$ext" >> "$out"
done < "$in"
exit 0
```
